clips.stepText: In your school, the council writes rules, prefects enforce them, and the principal settles fights. Splitting those three jobs stops one person from becoming a bully.

clips.stepText: First comes the law-making team, because every rule must start somewhere. Think of a family meeting deciding house rules and pocket money. In Nigeria, the National Assembly has two chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Together they pass bills, approve budgets, and investigate waste.

clips.stepText: Laws on paper do nothing until someone puts them to work. That is why we have the executive. Picture a compound head making sure everyone actually sweeps the yard on Saturday. The President leads this team for Nigeria, using ministers and civil servants to run schools, roads, and policing.

clips.stepText: What happens when a citizen says the government broke its own rule? You need a neutral referee, like an umpire in a football match. The judiciary plays that role. Courts listen to both sides, explain what the law means, and can cancel unlawful government acts. Keep that in mind.

clips.stepText: Why not let the same person sit in parliament and also serve as a minister? Because judging your own work is never honest. Suppose a class rep marks their own homework. Nigeria forbids that mix. If a lawmaker becomes a federal minister, they must leave their parliamentary seat immediately.

clips.stepText: Separation alone is not enough if one branch runs wild. Think of three market union officers who each hold one key to the cash box. The President can refuse a bill. Parliament can override that refusal with two-thirds support. See how the court can stop both? That mutual watch is checks and balances.

clips.stepText: Let us work through a classic question together. Imagine the President refuses to sign a bill into law. How can lawmakers push it through? Before guessing, recall why checks and balances exist. We must not let parliament bypass the President too easily, so a tiny vote will not work.

clips.stepText: Let us knock out the wrong choices one by one. The Senate alone with a simple vote is too weak. The Chief Justice cannot help, because judges interpret laws and never sign bills. A referendum will not work either, because referendums are for creating states. That leaves a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

clips.stepText: Check each pair carefully. Lawmakers do not appoint Governors, because voters elect them. Signing bills and commanding the army are powers of the President, not parliament. Issuing writs and voiding laws belong to judges in court. Only confirming ministers and investigating public spending are real legislative checks. Notice how knowing each branch stops careless mistakes.

clips.stepText: Here is a huge exam trap. Students often think the Supreme Court removes a President during impeachment. Not true! In Nigeria, lawmakers start and finish impeachment with two-thirds votes. The Chief Justice only picks the seven-person panel to investigate. Even better, courts cannot question the lawmakers' final decision.

clips.stepText: Another trap is thinking separation means the three branches never talk. They interact constantly! The President signs laws, the Senate vets judges, and courts review statutes. What Nigeria forbids is one person holding two jobs across branches, like being a Senator and a Minister together.

clips.stepText: Keep this one picture in your head. Government splits into law-makers, law-doers, and law-judges so tyranny cannot grow. Each arm has special constitutional tools to block abuse by the others. Know who does what, and these exam questions become easy marks.

clips.stepText: Think of a village football tournament. Before kickoff, everyone agrees on one rulebook. Even the team captain and referee must obey it, or the match falls apart.

clips.stepText: Why do we need a highest rulebook? Because without one, leaders could rewrite rules whenever they wish. Suppose a market chairman tries to ban elections after winning once. Under section one, any law or order that fights the Constitution is immediately cancelled by the courts.

clips.stepText: Exam questions sort constitutions in two ways. First, is it written in one single book, or spread across unwritten customs and old laws? Second, how hard is it to change? Picture a school rulebook locked in a safe versus one written on a chalkboard. We compare those two ideas next.

clips.stepText: Let us look at Nigeria's own rulebook. It is written, meaning you can pick up one bound document and point to the exact page. Say a police officer stops a peaceful meeting. A lawyer can open Chapter Four, section forty, and show the judge the exact words in black and white.

clips.stepText: Notice how hard it is to edit Nigeria's Constitution! An ordinary law only needs a simple majority of members present. Changing the Constitution needs two-thirds of every member in both federal chambers, plus two-thirds of all state assemblies. Protecting human rights is even tougher, needing four-fifths! That special hurdle makes it rigid.

clips.stepText: Let us tackle a worked question on rigidity. We want to change a right in Chapter Four. Why should that be harder than passing a normal road-repair bill? Because rights protect every citizen from sudden majority moods. Keep that clue in mind as we eliminate the wrong choices.

clips.stepText: Now knock them out cleanly. A simple majority is for ordinary bills, not the Constitution. The two-thirds choice is the famous trap! Two-thirds works for most sections, not Chapter Four, section eight, or section nine. An executive order gives amendment power to the wrong arms. So four-fifths of each House, plus two-thirds of the State Assemblies, is the exact answer.

clips.stepText: Here is a JAMB-style practice question. Notice the core issue. A state law clashes directly with the Constitution. Remember who sits at the very top of Nigeria's legal ladder. Let us test each option against section one of the 1999 Constitution to see which one holds up.

clips.stepText: Check each choice against section one. The State Law cannot apply inside its own state, because the Constitution binds every state without exception. Both laws cannot stand side by side, because clashing laws cannot both be valid. Automatic amendment flips the hierarchy upside down. Only the void choice matches section one subsection three, making the conflicting part void.

clips.stepText: Watch this double trap in section nine! First, most sections need two-thirds, while state creation, section nine, and human rights need four-fifths in the National Assembly. Second, count all members, even empty seats! Skipping absent lawmakers is how many candidates pick the wrong fraction.

clips.stepText: Students often treat written and rigid as the same word. They answer two different questions! Written asks how the rules are packaged. Rigid asks how hard they are to change. Nigeria happens to be both written and rigid, because section nine blocks easy changes.

clips.stepText: Here is the core idea to carry into your exam. A constitution is not an ordinary law. In Nigeria, it is written in one supreme book, and section nine locks it with tough supermajorities. Remember those two rules, and constitution questions will never catch you out.

clips.stepText: At a busy junction, the red light stops the big man's jeep and the okada rider alike. Under the rule of law, no leader sits above the law.

clips.stepText: Why does the rule of law matter? Because power without rules turns into fear. Imagine a local chief who jails anyone he dislikes without a hearing. Nigeria blocks that through three pillars. Law sits above leaders, every citizen faces the same law, and independent courts settle disputes fairly.

clips.stepText: Let us see how those protections work on the street. Suppose police arrest a trader at a market. Under section thirty-five, she has the right to stay silent until she sees a lawyer. She must get written reasons within twenty-four hours and see a court within one or two days.

clips.stepText: Freedom is not just about avoiding jail. You also need room to speak, worship, travel, and earn a living. Think of a young graduate moving from Kano to Lagos to open a shop. Sections forty-one and forty-two protect her right to live anywhere in Nigeria without ethnic discrimination.

clips.stepText: Are human rights unlimited? No! Your freedom to swing your fist ends where your neighbour's nose begins. For example, during a deadly epidemic, the government can restrict large gatherings to save lives under section forty-five. And if officials abuse your rights, you can ask a High Court for protection.

clips.stepText: Let us work through a practical rights question. Remember why section thirty-five gives strict clocks. If police could hold suspects forever without seeing a judge, liberty would be a joke. Check the distance given here. Five kilometres is well inside forty kilometres. Keep that distance rule in mind.

The two-month choice is clever because two months appears in section thirty-five, yet that is for starting trial without bail, not first seeing a magistrate. Within forty kilometres, the answer is one day.

clips.stepText: Here is a practice question on a favourite exam distinction. Not every good promise in the Constitution works the same way in court. Check which Chapter each option comes from. Remember, section forty-six only unlocks the High Court for one specific Chapter. Let us test all four.

Freedom from discrimination sits in Chapter Four. That makes C the only right a citizen can carry straight to the High Court under section forty-six.

clips.stepText: Many students see 'right' ideas like free education or jobs and assume they can sue government in court tomorrow. Careful! Those sit in Chapter Two as guiding goals, not Chapter Four rights. Under section six subsection six c, courts can only enforce Chapter Four directly.

clips.stepText: Do not think a state of emergency wipes out all human rights. Look at the proviso in section forty-five. Even in an emergency, government cannot make an act a crime after you already did it. And any limit on liberty must still be reasonable for handling that emergency.

clips.stepText: Take away this one thread. The rule of law puts the Constitution above every leader. It treats every person equally. It also backs Chapter Four rights with independent courts. Know the arrest clocks, the Chapter Two split, and section forty-five limits.

clips.stepText: Think of being a full member of a family compound. Everyone protects your place there. In return, you help keep the compound clean and safe.

clips.stepText: Does simply being born inside a Nigerian hospital make a baby a citizen? Not by itself! Nigeria uses blood ties, not just soil. Suppose two foreign tourists have a baby in Abuja today. That baby is not a citizen by birth unless a parent or grandparent is Nigerian.

clips.stepText: What if someone has no Nigerian parent, yet wants to belong? There are two legal doors. A foreign woman who marries a Nigerian man can apply by registration under section twenty-six. A foreign engineer who lives peacefully in Enugu for fifteen continuous years can apply for naturalisation under section twenty-seven.

clips.stepText: Here is where students often slip up. Can a Nigerian hold two passports? Yes, if you are a citizen by birth! For example, a child of Nigerian parents born in London keeps both. But someone who naturalised must give up their old non-birth nationality within twelve months. And birth citizens can never be stripped of citizenship.

Roads and schools would collapse. Section twenty-four lists your duties, like paying tax promptly, while section fourteen tasks government with your security and welfare.

INEC must reject it! A valid party needs an Abuja headquarters, open membership, national symbols, and leaders from two-thirds of states.

clips.stepText: Before asking who makes which rule, count the levels in Nigeria's structure. Section two says Nigeria is one indivisible federation. Section three lists thirty-six states, Abuja as the Federal Capital Territory, and seven hundred and seventy-four local councils in total. Notice how every tier is named directly in the Constitution.

clips.stepText: How do thirty-six states avoid stepping on each other's toes? By dividing who writes which laws! Only the National Assembly prints currency or commands the army on the Exclusive List. Both federal and state assemblies share the Concurrent List, like revenue rules. Anything left off both lists goes to states.

clips.stepText: A huge diverse country needs fair sharing of jobs and money to stay united. Picture a family business sharing profits and manager posts across every branch. Section fourteen insists federal offices reflect all states, not a tiny clique. And section one-sixty-two pools revenue while giving resource-producing states at least thirteen percent.

clips.stepText: Why not handle every market stall and street drain from Abuja? Because Abuja is too far to inspect every borehole or motor park! clips.stepText: Here is a trap students often miss about creating local governments. Yes, a State House of Assembly starts the process under section eight subsection three. clips.stepText: Keep 'concurrent' and 'residual' apart! Concurrent means running together, so both Abuja and the States can make laws on those listed items. Residual means what is left over. If a matter is missing from both constitutional lists, it belongs strictly to the State House of Assembly.
